    • 2. Cardinality, countability, and non-negative sums

    2. Cardinality, countability, and non-negative sums#

    Measure theory repeatedly combines countably many sets and nonnegative quantities. Cardinality tells us which collections can be arranged in a sequence, while extended nonnegative sums let us add a family without first choosing an ordering. Together, these ideas supply the mechanism behind countable additivity and the model convergence theorems used later for integrals. While arbitrary nonnegative sums are not strictly necessary for developing Lebesgue integration theory, they are a very useful test case for dealing with "generalized sums" beyond the finite algebraic setting.

    After studying these notes, you will be able to do the following.

    • Compare cardinalities and recognize finite, countable, and uncountable sets.

    • Prove that standard unions, products, and images of countable sets are countable.

    • Define and estimate nonnegative sums over arbitrary index sets.

    • Interchange nonnegative sums and apply monotone and dominated convergence to families of numbers.
